# Subspaces, embeddings, and all that

## "Siri, make me a UMAP"

Before making spin art plots of tens (or perhaps hundreds) of thousands of 
dollars' worth of data, one might consider what precisely is happening under 
the hood. Usually, this is prompted by the similar events to any trip under
a hood -- "the machinery isn't doing what I want it to!" Fortunately, the tools
to diagnose typical UMAP disasters are cheaper than the OBD reader for a car.


## How the spin art works (or doesn't) 

Nonlinear dimension reduction schemes like tSNE and UMAP typically operate in 
_reduced dimensions_. Given a number of linear dimensions, tSNE and UMAP attempt
to maximize the separation of minimally similar data points and vice versa. The
raw data is usually _compressed_ by taking _linear combinations_ of _features_,
since the usefulness of the results depends upon how _similarity_ is measured.
(Trivia: the X and Y coordinates of a UMAP embedding change when you add a Z...)

For example, with a single-cell RNAseq dataset, the _features_ are transcripts,
the typical _compression_ is a principal components analysis (PCA) with 30 or so
dimensions, and often the defaults involve throwing away 80% to 90% of the data
by relying only on _highly variable_ features (HVG, "highly variable genes").

An old trick from noisy microarray expression experiments is to mask features.
An older trick from statistics is to mask off entire _combinations_ of features.
Suppose Factor 10 = 0.5 * GENE1 + 2.6 * GENE2 - 1.3 * GENE345. Now suppose that
Factor 10 is almost entirely dependent upon technical artifacts that we don't 
care about and don't want in our colorful main figure. We can simply drop it. 
The remaining dimensions are referred to as a _subspace_ of the original data.


# A concrete example: classifying leukemia by cell of origin 

Instead of a typical single-cell dataset, we are going to train a model on 
DNA methylation from leukemia patients and sorted healthy progenitor cells.
Modern evidence-based understanding of hematopoiesis (blood production) has 
settled around a scheme where hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) provide a lifetime
of blood supply, mostly by delegating the work to shorter-lived multipotent 
progenitors (MPPs). These in turn generate three major classes of primed 
progenitors: megakaryocyte-erythrocyte progenitors (MEPs), which make platelets
and red blood cells; granulocyte-monocyte progenitors (GMPs), which make what 
you would expect from the name; and lymphoid-primed multipotent progenitors, or
LMPPs, which seem to be where B and T cells come from (but also some other cell
types, it's all a bit mysterious). A diagram from Grant Challen's _Exp Hem_ 
paper is below; it will may clarify or further murky-ify the topic. 

[![Hematopoiesis, simplified](lineage.png){fig-align="left"}](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.exphem.2021.09.007)

If these cells refuse to differentiate and instead proliferate, that's leukemia.
Certain mutations occur repeatedly in leukemia, and patients are often assigned
to specific treatment based on the mutations observed in their disease. However,
[the cell from which their leukemia arose may better predict their responses](https://ashpublications.org/blood/article/141/13/1505/495015/Is-BCL-xL-the-Achilles-heel-of-AEL-and-AMKL). Historically, that has been harder to model, but the 
nice thing about 'epigenomic' assays is that they are great at recovering this.
The really nice thing about these assays is that they are cheap and fast, too.


## Modeling normal and abnormal progenitors

Let's pull in the raw data from 120 leukemia patients and 5 healthy donors. 
The healthy donors provided bone marrow which was then sorted to yield MEP, 
GMP, and LMPP fractions (separated on the basis of cell surface antigens). 
The data is summarized as DNA methylation fractions across genomic coordinates,
and the column names indicate who is who and what is what. 

```{r}

aml <- read.csv(url("https://trichelab.github.io/data/aml.csv"), row=1)
meta <- data.frame(do.call(rbind, strsplit(colnames(aml), "_")))
names(meta) <- c("ID", "status", "lineage")
with(meta, table(lineage, status))

```

We can immediately observe two things:
* The control set (MEP, GMP, LMPP) is balanced. 
* The interesting set (leukemia patients) is severely imbalanced.

Let's see how this impacts our downstream adventures. 


## Fitting the data 

Let's skip a few steps (more on this later) and fit an appropriate-dimensional 
nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF) model of the data. (Why NMF? Because you
can't have negative amounts of DNA methylation, among other reasons.) 

```{r}
library(RcppML) 
aml <- read.csv(url("https://trichelab.github.io/data/aml.csv"), row=1)
aml <- data.matrix(aml) 
fit <- nmf(aml, k=5, seed=42, maxit=100)

library(ggplot2)
# plot the fraction of weights assignable to control vs. case data

```
